title: Orchestrated Restore Blueprint and Upgrade Notes
content:
TL;DR: This is a pragmatic, rehearsable blueprint for orchestrated restores and controlled upgrades for private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It combines a concrete restore checklist, Terraform module compatibility notes, and an upgrade choreography that minimizes downtime and preserves model/data integrity. Intended audience: SREs, deployment engineers, and solutions engineers running or supporting private customers.

Context and goals:
- Restore scope: full-site rehydration from object-store snapshots + db WAL, plus model artifacts and runtime caches.
- Upgrade scope: minor and major runtime upgrades (service binary, inference runtime, quantization tables, TF modules).
- Recovery objectives: RTO target = 2–6 hours depending on tier; RPO target = last successful snapshot (typically 15m–1h depending on customer SLA and storage).
- Non-goals: app-level data migrations that require manual reconciliation (those have separate runbooks).

Preflight (must run before any restore/upgrade):
1) Obtain change window approval and contact list (POC, SRE on-call, customer engineering lead).
2) Verify access: bastion credentials, KMS/HSM access, object-store admin credentials, terraform cloud token (if used).
3) Confirm snapshot inventory: list available snapshots and checksums (manifest in S3 path bucket://customer-snapshots/<cluster>/manifests/).
4) Validate terraform state access: ensure remote state lock available and tfstate bucket permissions are intact.
5) Acquire current infra map: ami/images, node labels, fleet sizes, region/cidr maps.
6) Take a final live snapshot (if cluster still partially healthy): db WAL + object-store manifest + inference cache dump (if feasible).

High-level orchestrated restore steps:
A) Prepare recovery environment (30–60m)
  - Spin up a recovery VPC/subnet or physical nodes isolated from prod. Use the saved terraform-recovery workspace.
  - Ensure policy: no external routing to production networks to avoid split-brain.
  - Restore remote state into a locked recovery tf workspace (copy state to recovery prefix).

B) Restore object storage (models, artifacts) (30–90m)
  - Locate manifest and preferred snapshot timestamp.
  - Use multipart parallel restore tool (we use s3-sync-rw or rclone) to copy artifacts into the recovery bucket.
  - Verify checksums (sha256 manifest compare).
  - If model weights are large and the customer uses on-prem artifact store, prefer a streaming restore to reduce disk pressure.

C) Restore database and WAL replay (45–120m)
  - Restore base backup to a standby node.
  - Apply WAL segments in chronological order. Example (Postgres):
    * pg_basebackup -D /var/lib/postgres -R -X stream -S recovery_slot 
      --write-recovery-conf -h source-host -U repl_user
    * Use pg_wal replay or pg_restore of logical dumps for schema-only restores.
  - After replay, run verification queries (count checks, sample rows).
  - If schema migrations are required by the new runtime, defer until after smoke tests or run in a controlled, reversible manner.

D) Recreate runtime components (30–90m)
  - Apply Terraform recovery workspace to bring up the control-plane components, similar layout as production but scaled-down.
  - Attach restored object-store and point config to the restored DB.
  - Start minimal services (auth, model-manager, scheduler) before starting inference nodes.

E) Model index + KV cache warm-up (variable)
  - Rebuild model indices if necessary. For LLM KV caches, either restore cached shards (if snapshot contained them) or allow warm-up via staged traffic.
  - For large caches, populate using background tasks with priority throttles to avoid IO saturation.

F) Validation and smoke tests (15–45m)
  - Execute test-suite: health endpoints, a small sample generation set, embeddings consistency, and end-to-end latency checks.
  - Verify signature checksums for model outputs against expected hashes where available.
  - Run regression prompts from the customer-supplied prompt-set.
  - Confirm metrics ingestion: token rates, error rates, latency histograms.

G) Cutover and routing (dependent)
  - If restoring for failover: update DNS / loadbalancer weights to point to recovery cluster; monitor for errors and rollback plan.
  - If restoring for validation only: keep recovery cluster isolated and share results with customer before final migration.

Terraform module notes (compatibility and gotchas):
- State separation: recovery workspace must use a different remote state prefix and explicitly not overwrite production tfstate. We recommend the following pattern in modules: var.remote_state_prefix and a safety flag var.disallow_prod_write.
- Provider versions: pin provider versions in the module root (aws, azurerm, google). Upgrades of providers can change resource lifecycle (notably LB and route resources).
- S3/GCS backend locking: ensure consistent locking via DynamoDB or GCS native locking; if locking fails, force-lock policy and run a tf state mv into the recovery prefix.
- Resource name templating: modules should accept a suffix var.env_suffix to avoid name collisions when recovery runs in the same cloud account.
- Sensitive outputs: do not export plaintext secrets. Use KMS-wrapped outputs. Recovery runbooks must explicitly request KMS unwrap credentials.
- Example tf snippet to copy state safely:
  * aws s3 cp s3://prod-tfstate/env/terraform.tfstate s3://recovery-tfstate/env/terraform.tfstate --profile recovery-admin

Upgrade choreography and safe rollouts:
- Upgrade types and risk profiles:
  1) Minor runtime (patch): low risk, can be canaried via rolling restart across nodes.
  2) Inference engine change (kernel selection / quantization): medium risk — requires validation prompts and perf benchmark.
  3) Major platform upgrade (db schema, tf module change): high risk — requires staged rehearsal in recovery cluster.

Safe upgrade pattern (for major):
1) Create a recovery cluster from prod snapshot (use above restore steps).
2) Apply new terraform module changes in recovery workspace; run tf plan and manual review.
3) Deploy upgraded runtime to a subset of inference nodes. Run full QA and perf tests.
4) If ok, run a canary in prod: route 1–5% traffic to upgraded nodes for 1–2h. Monitor errors, latencies, and quality regressions.
5) Gradually increase traffic with automated health gates. If any gate fails, rollback by re-routing and reverting terraform or using previous container image tag.

Operational scripts and snippets (examples):
- list snapshots: aws s3 ls s3://customer-snapshots/<cluster>/ --summarize | grep manifest
- verify checksum (bash): sha256sum -c manifest.sha256 || echo "checksum mismatch" && exit 1
- parallel restore (rclone): rclone sync s3:customer-snapshots/<cluster>/models recovery-s3:models --transfers=32 --checkers=16
- terraform copy state: terraform state pull > tfstate.json && aws s3 cp tfstate.json s3://recovery-tfstate/

Post-restore verification matrix (quick checklist):
- Services: all control-plane services healthy (api, auth, model-manager).
- DB: row counts in key tables within expected delta.
- Artifacts: model artifact checksums match manifest.
- Inference: sample response correctness and latency within SLA.
- Observability: logs flowing to recovery cluster's logging sink; metrics tagged with recovery prefix.
- Security: access logs show only authorized IPs; KMS decrypt operations logged.

Rehearsal cadence and SLAs:
- Quarterly dry-run: run a full restore in recovery workspace at least once per quarter for high-tier customers.
- Monthly smoke restores for mid-tier (subset of data).
- Post-upgrade rehearsal: any major runtime change requires a rehearsal within a dedicated recovery window.

Escalation and communications:
- Primary on-call: SRE team (rotate) — see team rota link in linked_artifacts.
- Customer escalation: solutions-engineering@redwood.ai and account exec.
- Exec notification: if RTO > SLA target for >2 hours, page director-of-ops.

Known caveats and open questions (tracking):
- Some customers use local NFS-backed model stores which do not snapshot atomically with object-store snapshots — need a filesystem quiesce step (TODO: add per-customer NFS quiesce script).
- Terraform module drift: resource rename in older modules can prohibit straightforward state import; maintain a mapping table (TODO: generate script to map old->new resource names).
- KV cache restoration: restoring cached shards can lead to inconsistent runtime behavior if not version-aligned with runtime binaries — prefer warm-up unless explicit compatibility is guaranteed.

Postmortem and learning loop:
- Every rehearsal and actual DR event must produce a brief postmortem (1–2 pages) with action items and ownership.
- Track flaky steps (those that took longest or had manual rework) and add automation where >2 manual ops repeat across runs.

Appendix: quick recovery terraform workspace example
- workspace vars: recovery=true, remote_state_prefix=recovery-<customer>, env_suffix=-rec, disallow_prod_write=true
- sample command: TF_WORKSPACE=customer-rec terraform init -backend-config="bucket=recovery-tfstate" && TF_VAR_env_suffix=-rec terraform apply -auto-approve

Open action items (short):
- [ ] Add NFS quiesce/flush helper to toolkit (owner: Daniel Rivera)
- [ ] Add automated checksum verification to restore pipeline (owner: Maya Chen)
- [ ] Draft customer-facing DR checklist (owner: Zoe Martinez)
- [ ] Create terraform resource-name-mapping generator (owner: Priya Kapoor)

Notes to self: this doc is intentionally pragmatic and should be used as the canonical rehearsal blueprint until we move cleaned procedures into Confluence. Keep doc minimal and update after first two rehearsals with timings per customer.

Unresolved: should model-weights be restored on-disk or streamed on first use by default? Streaming saves space but increases first-requests latency — flagging for product discussion.

End of draft.
